paragraph: Pairing behavior with detection fixes the target but introduces a cost problem. To compare two versions on valid-and-detected yield, an evaluator must execute behavioral suites for the emitted candidates, and in realistic settings many of those executions are expensive, unavailable, or pending. Two observations make this problem tractable and, at the same time, show why the obvious shortcuts are unsound. First, versions often emit byte-identical candidates for the same task, so many version rows assert the same behavioral fact. On sanitized MBPP, a comparison of two SEW~\cite{sew2026} versions involves 2,522 candidate rows that still need behavioral evidence, but only 1,138 distinct behavioral facts, and only three of them have different detected weight in the two versions. Second, identical candidate bytes are not enough to identify the fact. In a targeted study of the pinned SEW implementation, 13 groups of byte-identical candidates receive different validity labels because they are judged against different references, and in the CREST cohorts, correcting a namespace collision in the test harness changes ten labels without changing a single source file. A cache keyed by candidate text would merge different propositions; a cache keyed by version would refuse to reuse identical ones.

\subsection{Code watermarking and its evaluation}
Software watermarking predates neural code generation. Early schemes embedded identifiers in control flow, object structure, program state, or source-level transformations, and were evaluated for stealth, robustness, and resistance to semantics-preserving attacks~\cite{collberg1997,venkatesan2001,stern2000,monden2000,collberg2002,nagra2004}. Two lessons from that literature carry over. The transformation is constrained by the behavior the program must preserve, whatever the detector does, and robustness is always relative to a transformation class and attacker model rather than an intrinsic property of a detector score.

Regression-test selection avoids re-executing tests that a change cannot affect. Our stopping objective also differs from preserving every test outcome. The primary construct is behavior under a finite contract, not semantic equivalence. HumanEval and MBPP suites can miss faults~\cite{liu2023evalplus}, and their assertion styles differ. We make the exercised proposition explicit in $\kappa$, qualify every reference before admitting candidate evidence, retain assertion and exception witnesses, and run a separate expanded-input observer, which finds no comparable disagreement and leaves 95 pairs unavailable. Detector positivity is likewise specific to the released detectors and operating points. The generated cohorts participated in the upstream detector-development path, so their detector outcomes are operating-point observations rather than held-out accuracy estimates. On unwatermarked programs the released decisions stay near their operating points, but SEW false positives recur on the same programs across keys, so per-key rates must not be combined as if keys supplied independent evidence. The claim supported here is the disagreement between a released detector decision and an executed behavioral contract.
